questions.q: List the five distinct geographical settings in "I Sell My Dreams" in chronological order of the narrator's experience (not story order).
questions.a: Correct answer: Vienna (first meeting, 34 years ago) → Havana (opening disaster, present) → Barcelona (meeting with Neruda, 13 years after Vienna) → Oporto (Frau Frieda's retirement, mentioned in Barcelona) → Havana again (disaster aftermath, present). A wrong answer reveals the student cannot distinguish narrative time (flashbacks) from story time, or misses Oporto as a setting because it's only described in dialogue, not visited.

questions.q: Explain how the atmosphere of the Vienna tavern scene differs from the Havana hotel terrace scene, and why Marquez contrasts them.
questions.a: Correct answer: Vienna tavern — "straitened circumstances," "poverty-stricken regime," "beery euphoria," dim, crowded, student poverty; Havana terrace — "bright sun," "cheerful Cuban volunteers," breakfast luxury, then sudden violence. Marquez contrasts them to show Frau Frieda's power transcends class: she moves from buying meals for poor students to controlling a wealthy Viennese family. A wrong answer describes only physical differences (indoor/outdoor) without linking atmosphere to Frau Frieda's role or the magical realism theme.

questions.q: In the Barcelona section, the narrator says Frau Frieda lived in a "fake castle on a hill, from which one could see all the way across the ocean to the Americas." Apply the concept of magical realism to explain why this description is more than just setting detail.
questions.a: Correct answer: The "fake castle" symbolizes Frau Frieda's constructed identity (false name, invented persona) and her supernatural reach — her dreams "crossed the ocean" to control the Viennese family's fortune from afar. The view "across the ocean to the Americas" foreshadows the Havana disaster where her ring identifies her body. Magical realism uses realistic settings (a real castle in Oporto) to suggest supernatural connections. A wrong answer treats it as mere geographic description or misses the symbolic link between the castle's artificiality and Frau Frieda's "stratagem for surviving."

questions.q: Analyze how the sensory imagery of the wave disaster ("hailstorm of glass," "embedded one of them in the side of the hotel," "body of a woman secured behind the steering wheel by a seat belt") creates an atmosphere that bridges reality and fantasy.
questions.a: Correct answer: The imagery uses hyper-realistic violence ("not a single one of her bones was left whole," "boots ripped apart") to ground the supernatural event (a wave leaping a two-way street) in visceral physicality. The seat belt detail — modern, mundane safety device — contrasts with the ancient, magical serpent ring. This juxtaposition is Marquez's signature: the fantastic enters through precise, almost clinical realism. A wrong answer focuses only on the horror/gore or only on the wave's impossibility, missing how their fusion creates magical realism's atmosphere.

questions.q: Evaluate the narrator's claim: "Vienna was still an old imperial city... turned it into a paradise of black marketeering and international espionage." Is this atmosphere historically accurate or a narrative device? Justify.
questions.a: Correct answer: It's both. Historically, post-WWII Vienna was divided into four occupation zones, a hotbed of espionage and black markets — Marquez (who lived in Europe) knew this. But narratively, this atmosphere makes Frau Frieda's dream-selling plausible: in a city where reality is "more sinister than nightmares," a dream-seller becomes a rational survival strategy. The atmosphere justifies the magical element. A wrong answer says "it's just history" (missing narrative function) or "it's just fiction" (missing historical grounding that makes magical realism work).

questions.q: Create a 50-word atmospheric description of a new setting where Frau Frieda might have sold dreams before Vienna, using Marquez's style: blend specific sensory details with one surreal element.
questions.a: Good answer example: "In a Cartagena courtyard house smelling of fried plantains and salt, where lizards darted across whitewashed walls, Frau Frieda told a merchant's wife her son would choke on a mango seed — he did, three days later, and the seed sprouted a tree that bore fruit in December." Shows: specific sensory details (plantains, salt, lizards, whitewashed walls), realistic consequence (choking), surreal twist (tree fruiting out of season). Poor answer lacks sensory grounding or uses cliché magic (glowing eyes, floating) without Marquez's matter-of-fact tone.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Setting in "I Sell My Dreams" refers to the specific geographical locations (Havana, Vienna, Barcelona, Oporto) and temporal periods (post-WWII Vienna, 1970s Havana) where the narrative unfolds, while atmosphere is the emotional mood — magical realism's blend of surreal wonder, ominous foreboding, and nostalgic melancholy — created through sensory details like the "bright sun" shattered by a "huge wave," the "straitened ______" of student poverty, and the "fake castle" overlooking the ocean.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're describing a place that feels "haunted" without using that word — you'd ______ cold air, flickering lights, silence.
What is Setting in "I Sell My Dreams"? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Setting in "I Sell My Dreams" refers to the specific geographical locations (Havana, Vienna, Barcelona, Oporto) and temporal periods (post-WWII Vienna, 1970s Havana) where the narrative unfolds, while atmosphere is the emotional mood — magical realism's blend of surreal wonder, ominous foreboding, and nostalgic melancholy — created.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Setting in "I Sell My Dreams" refers to the specific geographical locations (Havana, Vienna, Barcelona, Oporto) and temporal periods (post-WWII Vienna, ______s Havana) where the narrative unfolds, while atmosphere is the emotional mood — magical realism's blend of surreal wonder, ominous foreboding, and nostalgic melancholy — created through sensory details like the "bright sun" shattered by a "huge wave," the "straitened circumstances" of student poverty, and the "fake castle" overlooking the ocean.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Setting in "I Sell My Dreams"?
questions.a: Students treat setting as "background" — a passive stage where events happen.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify all five distinct settings in the story, extract sensory details that establish atmosphere in each, and explain how Marquez uses setting shifts to structure the magical realism narrative — specifically how ordinary places become sites of supernatural intrusion.
